World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: ICC fugitive flees Philippine Senate after shooting chaos
World.content:
A Philippine politician wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) has escaped the country's Senate building, where he had been hiding out to avoid arrest.

Senator Ronald dela Rosa's escape from the heavily guarded building came after multiple gunshots were heard on Wednesday night.

The Senate was forced into lockdown and people inside ran for cover as the shots rang out.

Police are now investigating whether the shooting was instigated to help Senator dela Rosa slip out of the Senate.

Police officers stand outside the senate building after gunshots were heard inside. (REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez)

The 64-year-old had been under the Senate's protection and hiding out in his legislative office since Monday, when the ICC confirmed it was seeking his arrest on charges of crimes against humanity.

Senator dela Rosa was formerly the country's police chief, during which time he oversaw former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte's deadly "war on drugs".

Shots fired in Philippine Senate Authorities are still trying to work out who fired the gunshots heard inside the Senate building in the Philippines, prompting people to run for cover.

The ICC confirmed on Monday its warrant charges Senator dela Rosa with the crime against humanity of the murder of "no less than 32 persons" between July 2016 and the end of April 2018.

The shooting came hours after Senator dela Rosa had appealed on social media for his supporters to mobilise, claiming law enforcement officers were on their way to arrest him.

He has denied any wrongdoing, and filed an emergency petition with the Supreme Court in the Philippines on Wednesday urging it to block any attempt to transfer him to The Hague.

But Philippine Senate President Alan Peter Cayetano confirmed his ally had escaped the Senate, where he had been taking refuge.

“There is no obstruction of justice,” he said.

He read a text message from Senator dela Rosa's wife, Nancy, which apologised for the turmoil that his presence in the building had created.

"It's for this reason I'm sure Ronald made his escape," the message said.

The message did not disclose Senator dela Rosa's whereabouts, but said fleeing "was not part of the plan".

Military personnel in camouflage enter the Senate building on Wednesday night. (REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez)

Police spokesperson Randulf Tuano said investigations were underway to determine who was behind the shooting, with bullet casings and assault rifle magazines recovered.

He said one person had been detained, and had "provided names" that were being verified.

National Bureau of Investigation chief Melvin Matibag said the possibility that the incident was staged was also part of the probe.

Philippine Senate leadership has obstructed justice, analyst says

Political analyst Richard Heydarian told ABC's The World Senator dela Rosa's arrest should have been imminent.

"Right now we're getting conflicting messages whether there was a shooting between a supposedly unidentified group of people … or whether there actually was a failed apprehension or arrest operation," he said.

"Trust is very low, and there's a lot of suspicion.

"People are wondering whether that was just a fig leaf or a cover to allow Senator dela Rosa to escape."

Military personnel in camouflage enter the Senate building on Wednesday.

Mr Heydarian said many are demanding the Senate face legal ramifications for their role in blocking Senator dela Rosa's arrest.

"The Senate, or the leadership of the Senate, has been in obstruction of justice," he said.

"In fact, some are saying maybe the leadership of the Senate should face legal ramifications for blocking the enforcement of this valid arrest.

"This is precisely why the ICC is coming in, because there's a concern, as long as he is in the Philippines, [that] he's going to be protected."

Parents of those killed 'thirsty for justice'

Protesters had been gathering outside the Senate prior to the shooting, demanding the arrest of Senator dela Rosa.

Among them were the parents of people killed in the country's "war on drugs".

Llore Pasco, the mother of two men killed in the anti-drug campaign, said the spectacle of a powerful politician being granted due process and political protection stood in sharp contrast to the fate of her sons.

"That's how it is. If you are rich and powerful, even if you are at fault, you are still protected," the 71-year-old said.

"Surrender and face the crimes you're accused of, if you really have no guilt.

"There is a process, that's what you call due process."

Police personnel stand behind their shields outside the Senate in Manila. (AP Photo: Gerard Carreon)

Dahlia Cuartero, whose son was killed in 2019, said the ICC had given her and other victims a voice they never had in the Philippines.

"Justice in this country is really only for the rich. For us poor people, we have nothing to rely on," she said.

" We are thirsty for justice. "

Vice President Sara Duterte is in The Hague visiting her father, and likened Mr dela Rosa's case to what she called her father's "illegal abduction".

"What we are seeing now is the administration using all government resources to demolish political opposition," she said, in comments shared by her office.

She is also facing her own impeachment trial in the Senate on separate matters.

Reuters/AP

World.title: UK minister Wes Streeting quits, piling pressure on PM Starmer
World.content:
UK cabinet minister Wes Streeting has quit his role as health secretary, piling pressure on under-fire prime minister Sir Keir Starmer to stand down.

Sir Keir, who won a landslide election less than two years ago, is facing growing calls to quit following catastrophic local election results last week which saw the Labour Party lose almost 1,500 local council seats to its opponents.

Mr Streeting is widely viewed as a potential leadership candidate, and his allies say he is preparing a tilt for the top job.

UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer is under enormous pressure from within his party to quit. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

"It is now clear that you will not lead the Labour Party into the next general election and that Labour MPs and Labour Unions want the debate about what comes next to be a battle of ideas, not of personalities or petty factionalism," Mr Streeting said in a letter to the prime minister published on X.

He went on: "You have shown courage and statesmanship on the world stage — not least in keeping Britain out of the war in Iran.

" But where we need vision, we have a vacuum. Where we need direction, we have drift. "

Another likely challenger, former deputy prime minister Angela Rayner, said on Thursday that she had reached an agreement with tax authorities to clear up questions about her taxes that forced her to leave the cabinet last September.

While Mr Streeting comes from the moderate wing of the centre-left Labour Party, as does Sir Keir, Ms Rayner is a favourite of more left-wing voters, calling on the party to do more to boost the minimum wage and raise taxes on the rich.

Ms Rayner told the Guardian newspaper that Sir Keir should "reflect on" his position, adding that she was ready to "play my part" in any leadership election if Mr Streeting were to trigger a contest.

Former deputy prime minister Angela Rayner could launch her own bid for the Labour leadership. (Reuters: Chris J Ratcliffe)

Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham is also widely seen as a potential candidate, though he would have to find a way back into parliament before he could run.

Mr Burnham cancelled his regular Thursday appearance on a local BBC radio program this week to "prioritise discussions arising from last week's elections."

Allies have suggested a sitting member of the House of Commons could resign to make way for Mr Burnham to run in a special election.

Starmer vows to fight any challenge

Sir Keir, who won an overwhelming majority in the 2024 general election, is attempting to weather a string of ministerial resignations and scores of MPs' demands that he set out a timetable for his exit.

Starmer faces more calls to quit as ministers resign Sir Keir Starmer is striking a defiant tone, despite a growing number of his Labour colleagues urging him to step down.

A large majority of voters are frustrated with his government, which has failed to deliver on pledges to boost economic growth and improve living standards for working people, in part due to stubbornly high consumer price inflation.

He has told allies that he will fight a leadership challenge should a rival stand against him, warning colleagues that any leadership contest would plunge the government into "chaos" at a time it should be focused on issues like the cost-of-living crisis and the war in the Middle East.

Under Labour Party rules, any potential challenger to the prime minister would have to have the backing of 81 of the party's 403 MPs to make it onto the ballot.

More than that number have publicly called on Sir Keir to quit in recent days.

AP/ABC

World.title: 'Make a choice': Taylor defends comments aimed at non-citizens
World.content:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has denied permanent residents who are not Australian citizens will be targeted under any potential future Coalition government.

During his budget in reply speech on Thursday night, Mr Taylor singled out that group.

"We will remove Labor's handouts for non-citizens," Mr Taylor told parliament.

"Many Australians would be surprised to learn that non-citizens are eligible for welfare.

"We've already announced that the first homebuyer 5 per cent deposit scheme will be reserved for Australian citizens only. That's because Labor has allowed some 50,000 non-citizens to access this scheme."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers the day after delivering the Federal Budget. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Taylor told 7.30 his focus was on putting Australian citizens first, rather than targeting immigrants.

"It's about putting Australian citizens first," Mr Taylor said.

"I think it's extraordinary at at a time like this that the government has cut support for older Australians' private health insurance and yet there is welfare for Anglo-Australian citizens."

"Citizenship is a privilege and it's something we want people to get something from.

"If you contribute to this country, we want to contribute back and that's what citizenship is all about but when someone can get all the benefits without that, it becomes meaningless."

Mr Taylor added that some non citizens have access to what he said were "17 different" welfare programs.

People from Chinese and Indian diasporas — often have to give up their citizenship to become Australians.

Asked for his message to those people, Mr Taylor denied they would be made to give up anything.

"We're not forcing anyone to give up anything," Mr Taylor told 7.30.

"We're saying if you want access to the privileges which we believe should be privileges of citizenship, you need to become a citizen.

"You need to make a choice.

"The idea someone should arrive and the moment they arrive here get access to family tax benefit for instance, I think for Australians that's just not on at a time like this when we're really struggling."

Asked if that might affect the number of skilled migrants wanting to come to Australia, Mr Taylor said he did not believe that was the case.

One Nation has long spoken about lowering immigration numbers. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"There's always a long queue of people wanting to come to this country," he told 7.30.

"I believe it's the greatest country on Earth.

"If people come to this country in order to to receive welfare in the first couple of years of being here, perhaps that's not an appropriate circumstance.

"it's appropriate that people come spend some time and become a citizen. That's how most countries in the world work."

The One Nation playbook

While Mr Taylor said that Australians are struggling, so is the Coalition.

One Nation has been on the rise and Barnaby Joyce has been revelling in the party winning the Farrer by-election. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi) .

For the first time in history the Coalition lost former leader Sussan Ley's seat of Farrer in a by-election that saw One Nation's David Farley claim the party's first ever lower house seat in federal parliament.

Asked how big the threat was from One Nation, Mr Taylor said his budget in reply speech was not about stopping any momentum One Nation has.

However, also appearing on 7.30 former Nationals leader Barnaby Joyce said the Coalition had copied from the One Nation playbook.

"I'd like to thank them for basically reading off the One Nation script," Mr Joyce said before commenting on skilled migration.

"As we know we've been bringing in about the population of Canberra a year. It sort of waned a little bit lately, but we just didn't have the houses, we didn't have the schools.

"We certainly didn't have the dams, we didn't have the universities, we didn't have the hospitals."

Asked if he thought Mr Taylor's speech would stop the flow of Australian voters towards One Nation, Mr Joyce had a simple answer.

"No."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Mannagh's heavenly night leads Cats to statement win over Lions
World.content:
Shaun Mannagh's career-best night has powered Geelong past Brisbane to flip the script in their AFL grand final rematch at the Gabba.

The Cats dynamo kicked five goals and had 30 disposals — both career-highs — as the visitors started hot, weathered the Lions' reply, then found another gear in a 17.15 (117) to 11.10 (76) win on Thursday night.

(Getty Images)

Mannagh, 28, is in just his third AFL season after finally winning a contract with the Cats and debuting as a 26-year-old after years of VFL dominance with Werribee.

There were shades of last year's MCG decider, only with roles reversed, as the Cats ripped the Lions to shreds in a dominant third quarter to set up the win and improve to 7-3.

Brisbane, who had won six of their previous seven games, dropped to 6-4.

Bailey Smith had 34 touches and 11 tackles to go with seven clearances and two goals, while Tom Stewart (17 intercept possessions) was great at the back, setting the tone for his side's stifling, workaholic defence.

Darcy Wilmot had 31 disposals and Charlie Cameron was lively with three goals to lead the Lions, but Hugh McCluggage was uncharacteristically sloppy to sum up Brisbane's fortunes.

Veteran Lion Dayne Zorko, who has missed time with a calf injury this season, was a late withdrawal as Chris Fagan instead promoted James Tunstill on a wet Brisbane night.

AAP

World.title: Miraculous try-savers hand NSW second straight Origin series win
World.content:
A series of brilliant try-savers by NSW has secured the Blues back-to-back Women's State of Origin series wins with a 14-10 victory over Queensland at Lang Park.

For the second straight year, the Blues secured the shield in Game II, with Isabelle Kelly, Jesse Southwell and Teagan Berry coming up with stunning last-ditch efforts to end the Queensland challenge.

The last of them, from Berry, came in the final seconds of the game, denying winger Jasmine Peters what would have been a game-tying try.

Referee Belinda Sharpe initially awarded a try to make it 14-14 and give Lauren Brown a sideline conversion to win the game, but the bunker intervened.

Replays showed Peters's feet grazing the sideline as she went into touch.

It was the third time Peters had been stopped at the last moment in the right corner, with Southwell's effort perhaps the best of the lot, coming just after the NSW halfback was sprawled on the turf with an apparent neck injury.

It came after the Blues dominated large chunks of the first half, but led only 8-6 at the break after Southwell failed to convert Jaime Chapman and Keeley Nizza's tries, before Queensland centre Rory Owen powered over and Brown slotted the extras.

A dummy-half sneak by Jada Ferguson on 43 minutes gave the Maroons their first lead of the game, but it did not last long as Jess Sergis hit straight back for the Blues.

The match then turned into a brutal arm wrestle as both teams ramped up their defence, with Peters repeatedly denied by Kelly in the 54th minute, Southwell three minutes later, and finally by Berry in the final seconds.

The third game of the series will be played on the Gold Coast on Thursday, May 28, with NSW eager to complete the clean sweep after captain Isabelle Kelly was left in tears following a close loss in Game III last year.

Coach John Strange told his team to "bottle this feeling" and a number of the Blues players were adamant they were keen to finish the job this year.

That third game will be played a day after the men's series opener in Sydney.

The teams for men's Origin I will be named after Magic Round, taking place at Lang Park over the next three days.

Look back at how Women's Origin II unfolded in our live blog below.

Live updates Women's Origin II: NSW Blues 14-10 Queensland Maroons J By Jon Healy Collapse all posts off Sort Sort posts Latest Select an option New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters Filter Posts All 54 Key Events 12 Highlights 5 Tries 5 Comments 1 All filters That's where we'll leave you J By Jon Healy (Getty) Well, another Women's Origin series is decided. We'll of course be back for Game III on the Gold Coast in two weeks' time, but there is A LOT of footy to go under the bridge before then. The next three days will give us three days of men's Magic Round and we'll bring you every moment live from Lang Park. The men's Origin teams will be named on Sunday and Monday ahead of their series opener in Sydney on May 27. So make sure you bookmark ABC Sport and don't change your internet dial. NSW's John Strange and Isabelle Kelly are in the hot seat J By Jon Healy Blues coach John Strange is in awe of his players' try-savers at the death. "Jesse [Southwell] just picked her up and threw her over the sideline. Teagan Berry through her body on the line and did everything possible to stop her getting over the line." Berry came onto the field early for Jayme Fressard and Strange says he had intended to bring Fressard back on through the middle, but it never eventuated. Captain Isabelle Kelly says she loves playing inside former Dragons teammate Berry. "I actually had full confidence in Flash. She always pulls out these freaky things she can do in attack ... but defensively I love having her next to me. "She's the ultimate competitor." Kelly was in tears after losing the 'dead' rubber in Game III last year, so you know she wants to complete the sweep this time. "I felt like [in previous years] we let the jersey down and didn't play as well as we could. We knew we could got o new levels and it's not over for us." Strange days J By Jon Healy It's a second straight series win for John Strange. Loading Instagram content 'That's Origin footy': Qld coach J By Jon Healy Queensland coach Nathan Cross is thrilled with his team's resilience, but in the end it was a matter of millimetres. "That's Origin footy, we had our chances and we just couldn't get it done." Cross says the "errors killed us". There were 16 of them from Queensland hands tonight, leading to a 57 per cent completion rate. "That's been the most disappointing part." The next game is on the Gold Coast in two weeks' time, and Cross says the equation is pretty simple for his team. "Holding the ball would be good. I think everyone can see there's a real good footy team there, we've just got to stop beating ourselves." Maroons captain Tamika Upton praises the Blues defence. "Credit to NSW, they turned us away a lot and that defence got them the win." Both teams were elite without the ball tonight. We'll stick around for the coaches' press conferences J By Jon Healy Beautiful moment on the sideline J By Jon Healy Blues prop Millie Elliott is just a few months removed from giving birth to daughter Gigi. And she's celebrating with the team on the sideline. She's posing for a photo with NSW and Roosters teammates (and podcast co-hosts) Keeley Nizza and Olivia Kernick, when Maroons back rower Romy Teitzel walks by. Elliott calls her over to join the picture. Teitzel has been teammates with Elliott in Brisbane and Newcastle. Blues skipper praises 'showcase for women's footy' J By Jon Healy NSW captain Isabelle Kelly is "stoked" with that effort. "Really don't have much words," she tells ABC Sport. "Queensland, every single year, it doesn't matter who they put on the field, they play for that jersey and play with a lot of pride." She praises the Queensland defence, saying coach Nathan Cross has injected some venom into that forward pack. "I thought it was a really great showcase for women's footy." Maroons rue woeful completions J By Jon Healy (AAP) Queensland prop Jess Elliston is operating a little bit French on ABC Sport radio, so I won't share all of it, but she sums it up simply. "It's really hard, really shit," she says. And she says it boils down to a shocking 57 per cent completion rate. "It's our errors unfortunately and that's on us," she says. "We've been given that seven-week block, the coaches have given us everything. That's on us." NSW HAS WON A SECOND STRAIGHT WOMEN'S ORIGIN SERIES!! J By Jon Healy (Getty) They say defence wins championships, and that's certainly the case tonight, with Jesse Southwell, Isabelle Kelly and Teagan Berry coming up with brilliant try-savers to secure the shield for the Blues tonight. "It just goes to show the culture we've built in NSW camp," Southwell tells ABC Sport. "Every single one of us would do anything to win and anything for each other." QUEENSLAND IS IN! BUT IT'S NO TRY!!!! J By Jon Healy But is it a try? Referee Belinda Sharpe says yes! The bunker is having a really close look, and this is going to be taken off her. The Maroons spun it right and once again Jasmine Peters has a chance to score, but again the cover defence is on point. This time Teagan Berry saves the day and the series, just putting Peters's feet into touch at the last second. (Getty) 69' Penalty Queensland J By Jon Healy The bomb is taken by Tamika Upton and she spins it out to Julia Robinson, who's hit high! The Maroons will start a fresh set on the attacking side of halfway with 90 seconds left in the game. 67' Manzelmann tries the miracle but falls short J By Jon Healy Emma Manzelmann comes on and sees space in front of the ruck, so she takes a scoot, but the Blues are thrilled with that because it's the last! Eventually Manzelmann runs out of room and she has to hand it over. 66' Dust-up! J By Jon Healy The Blues can't muster anything on the last tackle and Kezie Apps refuses to give the ball up. Lauren Brown gives her a shove and a few words, and Sienna Lofipo joins the fray. Then the bodies come flying in from everywhere! The Maroons' series is still alive. Just barely. 62' More dropped balls from Queensland J By Jon Healy Destiny Brill and Chantay Kiria-Ratu drop the ball in successive sets for the Maroons, keeping the Blues deep in their half of the field and not allowing Queensland to even fire a shot in attack. Crowd confirmed J By Jon Healy We had been hearing about 28,000 fans here tonight, but it definitely seems the weather has kept some away. Still, 23,846 is nothing to sneeze. Just shy of the record. 57' SOUTHWELL WITH THE TRY-SAVER! J By Jon Healy Teagan Berry fumbles the Chantay Kiria-Ratu bomb and Jasmine Peters swoops on it. Once again she has the tryline at her mercy, but Jesse Southwell arrives out of nowhere and pulls off a perfect try-saver to dump Peters into touch. Peters just needed to reach out, but the ball was glued to her torso and she couldn't get the ball to ground. 56' Jesse Southwell is down and in real pain J By Jon Healy The NSW halfback is brought down by Romy Teitzel. World.title: Calls for more education following the suspected death of 'Sammy' the seal
World.content:
Marine experts have called for greater education on aquatic life, following the death of what's believed to be a beloved Australian fur seal known to Mornington Peninsula locals as Sammy.

On Wednesday, Zoos Victoria said the Marine Response Unit was called to a rescue on the peninsula, south-east of Melbourne, where they found a deceased seal.

Zoos Victoria said it could not confirm whether the seal was Sammy as it did not have any original DNA samples for testing, but locals believe it was.

How the animal died is not yet known, but Zoos Victoria said tests were conducted that could reveal a cause in the next few weeks.

Sammy the seal rose to fame after Mornington Peninsula influencer Bec Watson created a Facebook page for the animal, posing as Sammy himself, stacking up over eight thousand followers.

Bec Watson is an online influencer based on the Mornington Peninsula, known for 'Bec's Unhinged Reviews.' (Supplied: Bec Watson)

"I gave him his little personality and I was almost narrating for him what he would feel — because I feel like he would be a sassy little seal," she said.

"He was just so cheeky, he'd get into so many troubling spots where you'd just look and go, 'okay it's his house now, we've just got to leave him, he owns that space'."

Sammy's fame was elevated further when a seal caused amusement on Point Nepean Road in Dromana by sunbathing on the road, delighting motorists despite causing delays.

Loading...

After Sammy's suspected death, Ms Watson said she was accused of contributing to the pinniped's death by encouraging members of the public to approach the animal, cause it distress.

" I turned into a little bit of someone to blame. "

The influencer defended her posts promoting Sammy, which included showing the seal's locations around the bay, saying she did not upload photos straight away and always maintained a safe distance when capturing photos of the seal — and encouraged others to do the same.

"I was almost doing it for other people to be able to see him online and not feel the need to go and visit him," she said.

The Instagram selfies putting people at risk

Jeff Weir is the Executive Director at the Dolphin Research Institute, a non-for-profit marine conservation organisation based in Hastings on the Mornington Peninsula's east coast.

Jeff Weir has researched marine life on the Mornington Peninsula for over 30 years. (Supplied: Jeff Weir)

He said while a majority of the public respect the behaviour of seals, some put the animal and themselves at risk.

"I've seen situations where, not so much the fur seals, but with an elephant seal and even a really sick leopard seal, [people put] their child on its back to take a photograph," he said.

" This sort of era of selfies, either being really close for yourself or doing something silly like putting your child on the back, is a very risky thing. "

Mr Weir said there were more people injured in Port Phillip Bay by seals than sharks.

"They're wild animals and they can be very aggressive and they can respond and people can get hurt."

Loading...

Seal population bouncing back after a dark past

Marine biologist at Deakin University, Saia Bartes, said the population of Australian fur seals was still recovering from the 1800s, when they were hunted to near-extinction, primarily for their pelts which were used for clothing, including hats and coats.

She said after spending several days foraging for fish, the marine mammal rests on land.

"They are recovering all the energy that they lost while travelling to eat," she said.

Saia Bartes spend several weeks researching Australian fur seals on islands in Bass Strait (Supplied: Saia Bartes)

While female seals often lay on the shore to lactate their pups, Ms Bartes said it was much more common to see males make their way inland.

" But I've never seen seals coming along the road, that was something new. "

Ms Bartes said there were several risks humans pose if they approached resting seals on land.

"If we are bothering the animal and not allowing them to sleep and rest and recover that energy, that would be detrimental to other activities," she said.

"It could also be that they are injured or they are sick."

A risk of disease transfer also existed between seals and humans, but also pathogens carried on pets like dogs, Ms Bartes explained.

"Even though they are really cute and really attractive … the best advice I can give to anyone would be to maintain a distance."

Sammy the seal was often spotted by locals sleeping in several locations around Victoria's Mornington Peninsula. (Facebook: Sammy the Seal)

Can social media be a safe education tool?

Reflecting after the seal's death, Bec Watson admitted she had had second thoughts about creating the social media persona for Sammy.

"In hindsight now, I know he was a wild animal and I probably shouldn't have made that about him," she said.

" I wouldn't do it again … I'm deeply sorry. "

Ms Watson agreed that more needed to be done to educate the public on seal safety, but said Sammy's Facebook page, despite its criticism, achieved that.

"So many people are on their phones, so many people are reluctant to pick up a book and do their research, I really thought [the Facebook page] is how we could get to people."

She said social media could still be used as a powerful tool to raise awareness of seals in the region, but stressed it should be done without disturbing the coastal creatures.

"We've got amazing phones with zooms, so we can be a very good distance away and just still get a pretty good photo."

World.title: Green light for Andrew Forrest's $70m Ningaloo Reef resort
World.content:
Mining billionaire Andrew "Twiggy" Forrest's plan for a $70 million luxury resort on the Ningaloo Reef has cleared its final approval hurdle, after years of delays and cutbacks.

In 2017, the Ningaloo Lighthouse Resort property, about 1,230 kilometres north of Perth, was snapped up by the magnate, who aimed to redevelop a rundown Exmouth caravan park at the site into an eco-tourism hotspot.

But the initial application to build an $85 million, 550-guest retreat was withdrawn while awaiting environmental and cultural approvals.

Nearly a decade passed while efforts to give the resort unfettered beach access were dumped by WA's Main Roads authority over fears it could damage an Aboriginal heritage site.

Andrew Forrest first submitted plans for the Ningaloo Reef site in 2017. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

A revised approach, submitted earlier this year to the local shire, reduced its footprint by $15 million dollars and about 400 guests.

The application was unanimously approved today by the WA Planning Commission, with minor amendments.

It is understood Z1Z Resorts, the accommodation arm of Andrew and Nicola Forrest's Tattarang company, is still working through the conditions in detail but has voiced a willingness to accept the changes before the assessment panel.

A spokesperson for the project could not confirm a timeframe for construction or opening.

"We look forward to working with the community as the project progresses," the spokesperson said.

Environmental concerns

The larger vision for the resort was given the green light by then WA Environment Minister Reece Whitby in 2023, subject to strict measures to protect wildlife and Aboriginal cultural sites.

At the time, the Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) recommended special lighting arrangements to minimise its impact on the sea turtles and shorebirds that lay their eggs along the World Heritage-listed Ningaloo coast.

The project, situated outside Exmouth and adjacent to the marine park, is unlikely to be assessed by the EPA again, as it has only decreased in size.

Current plans involve converting the heritage-listed Vlamingh Head lighthouse keepers' quarters into a hotel reception and constructing dozens of villas, a restaurant, and spa facilities.

A concept image of the Ningaloo Lighthouse Resort. (Supplied: Tattarang)

Almost four hectares of native vegetation will be cleared within the 45-hectare development.

The property still falls within a registered Aboriginal heritage area, Vlamingh Head, that has been a ceremonial and spiritual site for tens of thousands of years.

In its submission before the planning commission, Z1Z Resorts said it had obtained approval from the minister for Aboriginal affairs under Section 18 of Aboriginal Heritage Act 1972, and was consulting extensively with traditional owners.

Australian Marine Conservation Society chief executive Paul Gamblin previously opposed the development, but said it was now "heading in the right direction".

The Ningaloo Lighthouse Resort hopes to source potable water for the villas and plunge pools via groundwater bores, while wastewater will be recycled to irrigate the property.

The proposal fuelled unease for the region's already depleted groundwater stores and the fragile subterranean ecosystems that course through the limestone peninsula.

"If the current proposal stays within the existing footprint … but then also adopts contemporary energy and water efficient processes, and they should be absolutely world leading for an area like this, then that would be the appropriate approach," Mr Gamblin said.

Boost for cyclone-hit town

Exmouth Chamber of Commerce president David Gillespie also had groundwater concerns.

The state-run Water Corporation announced last year it would construct a seawater desalination plant in Exmouth by 2030, with the local drinking water scheme already approaching capacity.

"They've certainly got challenges around the infrastructure domain," Mr Gillespie said.

" It's just a matter of just how much money you throw at it to make it work. "

The tourist town of Exmouth in WA's north-west. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

Mr Gillespie said it was a welcome economic reprieve for Exmouth, which was still recovering from ex-Tropical Cyclone Narelle.

The category-four system made landfall over Exmouth in March, wrecking a huge swathe of homes and businesses, including its largest resort.

"Less beds is putting more stress on the other accommodators (sic) to accommodate everybody at this point in time," Mr Gillespie said.

"Exmouth itself is going to take at least 18 months to two years just to get back to some normality."

The controversial miner is no stranger to the town, having opened a multi-million-dollar marine research facility there in 2021.

"Once it's built and it's open for business, it doesn't matter who owns it, it will be a great asset to Exmouth," Mr Gillespie said.

World.title: Labor's 'jaw dropping' fracking decision wedges One Nation at first opportunity
World.content:
Since One Nation's breakthrough state election result in South Australia this year, Premier Peter Malinauskas has been striking a seemingly diplomatic tone about parliament's new conservative cohort.

Last Tuesday, as South Australia's seven new One Nation MPs prepared for their first day in parliament, the Labor premier said we should "welcome the fact that there are opposition parties in our state who have an important function to perform to hold us to account".

"I stand ready willing and able to work with opposition parties regardless of their political hue, regardless of our political differences, if it's in the best interests of the state," he said at the time.

"I've communicated that to [One Nation SA leader] Cory [Bernardi] directly."

High-minded civics, sure.

A sign that Labor will make One Nation's life easy in parliament? Absolutely not.

Just ask new One Nation MP Jason Virgo.

One Nation's Jason Virgo won the seat of MacKillop in a contest with the Liberal Party. (Facebook: Jason Virgo for MacKillop)

The South East MP has just been put into a political bind by the government's push to end the moratorium on fracking in his local electorate.

The 10-year ban was legislated by the former Marshall Liberal government in 2018 in response to community fears the gas extraction method would threaten groundwater and local agriculture.

Those community concerns have not dissipated, but neither has One Nation's zest for resource extraction.

Last month national One Nation party leader Pauline Hanson was spruiking "drill, baby, drill" on social media.

It leaves One Nation having to balance its traditional views with those of Mr Virgo's constituents.

Peter Malinauskas (right) greets One Nation's new MPs on the first day of parliament. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Labor, which argues ending the moratorium can be done safely and is necessary to shore up gas supplies in the 2030s, will accuse One Nation and the Liberals of being energy hypocrites if they keep the moratorium in place.

"The Liberal Party and One Nation talk a big game when it comes to energy sovereignty and security — well, now they have an opportunity to prove it," Mr Malinauskas said.

"Instead, I fear they may hide behind the veil of confrontation."

But the level of community angst will be hard for Mr Virgo to ignore.

Naracoorte-Lucindale Mayor Patrick Ross said his "jaw dropped" when he heard the government's plan, and he is already making his views known to the fledgling One Nation MP.

"I've made it very clear, and I know that other mayors in the seat of MacKillop have made it very clear, that first and foremost you must represent your constituents," Mr Ross said.

Naracoorte Lucindale Mayor Patrick Ross says "fracking is a no go". (ABC News)

"It doesn't matter where the party may sit [or] One Nation may sit on resources extraction, you must support the people who put you into the parliament, and that is the constituents.

"And they will be very loud and clear to Jason Virgo that fracking is a no-go for MacKillop."

An attempt at the middle path

Mr Virgo has already tried to find middle ground through the issue, calling for local consultation.

In a rare interview with 891 ABC Adelaide today, he said the moratorium was ending in 2028 so "there's no need to push it through today or next week".

One Nation's Jason Virgo Sixteen years before Jason Virgo won the SA seat of MacKillop for One Nation in the state's south-east, he twice ran for parliament as an Australian Sex Party candidate.

"Our community down here really wanted the country cabinet to come down and listen to the concerns that are facing our region, and instead what we've had is a bit of a slap in the face," he said.

Mr Virgo, who rejected that he was trying to walk on both sides of the street, said the eastern states should play a bigger role in gas extraction.

"Gas security is important and there is plenty of the state to drill for gas, we absolutely want gas," he said.

"But what I would suggest is that the Labor premier needs to get onto his Labor mates in the eastern states and get them to start drilling their fair share."

Liberal MLC Ben Hood, from Mount Gambier, made a similar call for consultation, while federal Liberal MP Tony Pasin told the premier to "frack off".

A second environmental battle

There are risks for Labor, too.

Ministers could face some fiery criticism as they try to explain their decision at a country cabinet forum in the South East tonight.

The move also draws attention to Labor's previous comments that it would not touch the fracking moratorium before 2028.

New independent Mount Gambier MP Travis Fatchen has already vowed to fight the proposal "every step of the way".

"Before the election in 2022, the premier gave a clear assurance to the people of the Limestone Coast that there would be no changes to the moratorium," he said.

"That promise has now been broken."

But Labor does not have much to lose in the South East either; the party has not held the seat of MacKillop since 1956 or Mount Gambier since 1975.

It is harder to imagine Labor wading into such a fraught environmental issue if they had a local MP fighting for re-election or were a realistic chance of winning a South East seat in 2030.

But it is also true that the government is fighting a separate environmental battle in an area where it does have a political stake.

Protesters outside SA parliament voice opposition to the North Adelaide Golf Course redevelopment. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

That is the seat of Adelaide, where debate continues to rage over the felling of 585 trees in the park lands for the government's $45 million redevelopment of the North Adelaide golf course.

Rather than One Nation, this political fight has been with the Greens, with thousands gathering on the steps of Parliament House last night to protest the redevelopment.

Nothing has put the government off course so far and the trees continue to come down. The premier is pointing to Labor's resounding victory in the seat of Adelaide as a mandate.

One Nation wedged, the Greens steamrolled and the Liberals struggling for oxygen?

It could be an indicator of the next four years to come.

World.title: How Zorko’s absence exposed Lions’ void and announced Cats as a flag favourite
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 How Zorko’s absence exposed Lions’ void and announced Cats as a flag favourite Nick Wright May 15, 2026 — 12:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan has conceded there is a void in his backline in need of filling – one which had a harsh light shone upon it in Dayne Zorko’s absence against Geelong. The veteran was a late scratching from his side’s 17.15 (117) to 11.10 (76) defeat to the Cats on Thursday night, and it appeared to completely shift the way his teammates rallied from the back. Dayne Zorko at a training session in Brisbane on Tuesday. Getty Images Zorko was only two weeks back from a calf concern and withdrawn from the grand final rematch to manage his workload. At 37, he is yet to announce any retirement intentions, and has continued to sign one-year contract extensions since 2022. Fagan hinted managing Zorko’s work would be a regular theme.



“He just pulled up sore from the game last week, and he wasn’t feeling 100 per cent at training on Tuesday, and he wasn’t any better at the captain’s run so we decided not to risk him,” the coach explained. “He’s 37, played 300 games, we’ve [gone] from a Sunday to Saturday to a Friday to a Thursday in the last month, and sometimes that catches up with the older guys, so we just wanted to be careful with him. “You’ve got to be sensible.” Chris Fagan and his Lions have some thinking to do. Getty Images The 311-game star’s career has undergone a renaissance ever since his shift to halfback in 2024. His service – and willingness to attack the corridor – has made the Lions a lethal counter attacking unit.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Privacy and security needs to be lifted’ but McCluggage defends Lions culture Before injury, Zorko had averaged more than 29 touches, four inside 50s and six rebound 50s a game. While Brisbane cruised to wins against Adelaide and Essendon without him, the Cats exposed his void. Aside from a Lions second quarter four-goal blitz – highlighted by two of Charlie Cameron’s three goals for the night, and a brilliant strike from a busy Levi Ashcroft (28 disposals) – Geelong rarely gave up the momentum. In the first quarter alone, they had 23 inside 50s to Brisbane’s eight, with Jeremy Cameron and Bailey Smith in outrageous touch – both kicking freakish snap goals around the body to give their side a 22-point buffer. Coming out of trouble, the Lions targeted the flanks to little avail and such moves were quickly nullified. The Lions’ only two goals both came from the rare occasions they were able to escape their half – 2025 draftee Cody Curtin, fresh off inking a contract extension to the end of 2029, found unmarked by Cam Rayner, before the latter scrambled on a loose ball to strike himself.



Loading Their all-star midfield was kept completely quiet, with Lachie Neale (six first quarter touches) in particular hardly sighted as Geelong rival Oisin Mullin kept him under his watch. Editor's pick Analysis

AFL 2026 The Cats have made a statement. They are the real deal yet again Once Cats forward Shaun Mannagh exploded – kicking five goals along with 30 disposals and three goal assists – there was never a chance of Brisbane mounting a definitive comeback. Four goals in seven minutes early in the third quarter extinguished much of the Lions’ hope. “We lost [Brandon] Starcevich to West Coast and [Noah] Answerth [to concussion] who are good checking defenders. Lincoln McCarthy we tried to develop to that, so the guys who had the job on him [Mannagh] tonight just didn’t get it done,” Fagan said.



“That doesn’t mean to say we can’t make those guys better. We’re asking guys like Jaspa [Fletcher] and Darcy [Wilmot] to play on him, and they’re probably more attacking halfback flankers, so they’ve got to get the balance right in when to attack and when to defend. Related Article NRL 2026 The schools and club talent factories producing the most NRL players “That’s the reality at the moment, we have to develop somebody into that position.” Without Zorko’s influence in generating go-forward, the Lions midfield was deprived of chances to strike, as marquee men Neale, Will Ashcroft (24 disposals) and Hugh McCluggage (16 disposals) were kept contained. In contrast, Mannagh and Smith (two goals, 34 disposals) were at their damaging best, to announce Geelong as serious flag threats and leave the Lions in a period of self-reflection. Not that Fagan is willing to “hit the panic button”, lamenting his side’s 59 per cent kicking efficiency was more a credit to the Cats’ pressure.



“I thought a lot of our really good players didn’t play as well as they normally do. Oisin was tagging Lachie Neale, but I don’t think some of our other mids were getting tagged too closely,” Fagan said. “They just didn’t have good nights. We’ve just won six of our last seven games … we’ve had three or four six-day turnarounds in a row, we just probably need to suck a bit of air in, get a bit of a rest and get ready to go again.” Fagan remained hopeful Zorko, McCarthy and Jarrod Berry could return for next Sunday’s clash with the Giants. World.title: The Cats have made a statement. They are the real deal yet again
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The Cats have made a statement. They are the real deal yet again Peter Ryan May 15, 2026 — 12:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

The Cats will never disappear. All the prayers, predictions and prognostications from opposition supporters have amounted to nothing. Shaun Mannagh celebrates one of his five majors for the night. Getty Images They are still there, nagging away like the lawn you haven’t mowed, the tail-light you haven’t fixed, or the dirty clothes staring back at you from the washing basket. Their demolition of their reigning premiers just five days after smashing Collingwood could be described as a statement, or a brutal reminder, or simply the perfect execution of a well-planned mission.



The club that has played in preliminary finals in eight of the past 10 seasons, and three of the past six grand finals, will be sniffing at the flag again. That’s the only conclusion that can be reached after their Thursday night throttling of the Lions. Bailey Smith and Tanner Bruhn were again influential for Geelong. AFL Photos Cats coach Chris Scott was content with the performance, but knows nothing memorable is won in May. “There is still a lot of footy to be played, but we are confident we will get better,” Scott said.



The Cats’ midfield is supposed to be a weakness but no one worth listening to has got that message through to them yet, except Port Adelaide, anyway. The combination led by young ruckman Mitch Edwards is workmanlike on paper, with rock star Bailey Smith surrounded by bass players in Tom Atkins, Tanner Bruhn, Shaun Mannagh and tagger Oisin Mullin. View post on X Star runner Max Holmes sits in defence to be called upon when needed, while Patrick Dangerfield just marches into the centre if an old and occasionally wise head is needed. Mullin kept dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale quiet, while Hugh McCluggage could not have his normal influence. Will Ashcroft was reasonable, but when Geelong dialled the volume up early in the third quarter none of those stars could be heard over the din as the Cats’ lead stretched to 42 points.



The Cats lost the clearance count but scored 31 more points from clearance than their opposition as they have made that a strength in the past six weeks. Jeremy Cameron kicked three goals for the Cats to take his season tally so far to 27. AFL Photos Mannagh, who was in a rut (a dirty word in some parts) six weeks ago when he described his game against the Hawks on Easter Monday as “a shocker”, has bounced back with vengeance. He was superb in the second half, kicking three goals in a three-minute-and-50-second burst that was perhaps the most exciting sub-four-minute stretch since Roger Bannister ran his famous mile. OK, that might be an exaggeration, but it was a great watch, nonetheless, with two of his goals coming from kicks out of midair. The Lions, with their dwindling supply of small defenders, had no answer. View post on X



One important swing from the grand final was that the Cats had Tom Stewart back in the team, while the Lions were without the injured Dayne Zorko. Stewart, who missed last year’s decider through concussion, intercepted marks and returned anything the Lions could fire inside 50 with interest. He was outstanding. He is commanding a defence that is desperate to keep their foot on their opponents’ throats, while the forward line is predictably unpredictable, with Jeremy Cameron and Shannon Neale the constants inside 50 as the game’s best coach feeds players through the forward half, with Jack Henry making a cameo as he returned from injury. Cameron kicked three to take his season tally to 27, the same number he had after round 10 last year. He finished with 88 goals in 2025. Chris Fagan and his Lions have some thinking to do. Getty Images The Lions will be in contention, too, with their coach Chris Fagan suggesting their hunger for the contest wasn’t as it had been recently with three six-day breaks in a row a potential factor. Justifiably, he said there was no need to “hit the panic button”. Fagan would be well aware the Lions had only lost once to the Cats in their previous five encounters heading into the match. “Well done Geelong. They were great,” he said. The reality is the Cats have been great with monotonous regularity over the past 20 years – their smarts and hard work still the benchmark for most clubs in the competition. They play another team with the same reputation, Sydney, next week at home in a game that will either elevate Geelong’s standing, or confirm the reality they live by, which is that every opponent is tough.



The most ominous comment came from Bailey Smith post-game when he spoke to Channel Seven after another excellent 34-disposal performance. “We don’t want to peak just yet,” Smith said. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Blues hold out Maroons in epic finish to secure Origin series victory
World.content:
Maroons 10, Blues 14

A try-saving tackle from Teagan Berry in the final minute has sealed a 2026 Women’s State of Origin series victory for NSW who have claimed their first back-to-back Origin titles since 2019.

The 14-10 victory for NSW at Suncorp Stadium means the Blues now have the chance to claim the first series whitewash since the three-match format was introduced to the women’s game in 2024, when they head to the Gold Coast for game three on May 28.

Loading

Suncorp Stadium was roaring as referee Belinda Sharpe awarded Maroons winger Jasmine Peters a try in the corner of the field to level the scores in the final minute. But, on second inspection, Berry had done enough, as the NSW speedster dragged Peters’ foot into touch before she managed to put the ball down.

Blues captain Isabelle Kelly said she never doubted Berry could save the match when all was on the line.

“I actually had full confidence in Flash [Berry]. I think she’s one of those players that will go right to the last minute, or she always pulls out these freaky things that she can do,” Kelly said.

“I think she’s known a lot for her attack, but defensively, I love having her next to me. I think she’s someone that will really aim up when she needs to.”

These one-on-one moments are what sealed victory for NSW in the end, with a try-saving tackle by Jesse Southwell keeping Queensland out of the match earlier in the second half, with Peters once again the victim of a desperate and determined NSW defence in that instance.

“Jesse just picked her up and threw her over the sideline, and then right at the death there, they passed the ball out and, and Teagan Berry threw her body on the line and did everything possible to stop them getting the try that was going to level the game,” Blues coach John Strange said.

“[Maroons halfback] Lauren Brown’s such a great competitor, and she would have loved that moment as a goalkicker to win the game for a state. But fortunate enough, Teagan did everything she could.”

Teagan Berry makes a try-saving tackle on Jasmine Peters in the final minute of Origin II. Getty Images

It was a phenomenal effort from Southwell, who looked to be in serious trouble just moments earlier after getting her head stuck in the turf following a tackle from Queensland’s Romy Teitzel and Rory Owen.

The NSW No.7 was awarded player of the match on Thursday night.

Tensions were running high after that as Queensland tried to get back in the match, with Maroons playmaker Brown and Blues front-rower Kezie Apps exchanging words and shoves as the Blues tried to secure the win.

But as the desperation ran high for Queensland, NSW continued to suffocate their attack. And, in the end, it was the Blues who walked away with victory after reclaiming the lead with a Jess Sergis try in the 46th minute.

Sergis had been powerful all night, and it was her effort from a scrum feed that put NSW on the board first as she teamed up with winger Jaime Chapman to open the tally for the Blues from a scrum feed.

With NSW stacked on the left, Southwell opted to throw the ball right, backing Sergis to draw in the Queensland defenders before Chapman finished it off in the corner.

Blues winger Jaime Chapman opens the scoring. Getty Images

That was before Keeley Nizza burrowed across from dummy-half to score and send NSW to the sheds at half-time with an 8-6 lead after Rory Owen kept the Maroons in the match.

The Maroons then scored first in the second half, with Jada Ferguson burrowing across between Abbi Church and Southwell to give Queensland the lead for the first time.

But Sergis had other ideas, as the Blues centre dragged Owen across to score what would be the eventual match winner and final try to hand victory to NSW.

For most of the match, Queensland beat themselves, with a poor completion rate – especially in the first half – coming back to bite them in the end.

“Errors killed us tonight. I think we were five or six errors and 57 per cent completion [in the first half], and you just can’t win footy games like that,” coach Nathan Cross said.

“I think everyone could see the footy team that we are when we hold the ball and complete, and start giving Meekes [Tamika Upton] a bit of space, and Chantay Kiria-Ratu some time to shine.

“I could see the style of footy that we trained so well for. I could start to see it coming out and showing in glimpses, but then that leads to another error, and then we’re sort of back in the washing machine again.”

The Maroons will have the chance to salvage a match in this series in a fortnight, which captain Upton said was crucial for such a young team.

“I think it would be really crucial for this group,” Upton said.

“It’s been two tight matches, which we haven’t been able to seal, and to be honest, that’s my job as a leader. None of them should have their head down in that room over there because they were outstanding on this stage.”

World.title: Mannagh shines in Gabba debut as Cats score statement win over Lions
World.content:
Geelong coach Chris Scott believes Shaun Mannagh could still have a long career despite his late start to AFL football.

The 28-year-old turned on a match-winning performance in tonight’s match with five goals and 30 disposals.

Cats coach Chris Scott and star midfielder Bailey Smith chat post-game in Brisbane. AFL Photos

Scott said he was proud of Mannagh’s development after working his way through the ranks into the AFL.

But he added that, physically, Mannagh’s body was strong and fresh, which could allow him to play for a long period of time.

World.title: Wes Streeting quits as minister, clearing way for challenge to Starmer
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeUK politics Wes Streeting quits as minister, clearing way for challenge to Starmer David Crowe May 14, 2026 — 10:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A senior British cabinet minister has quit the government to clear the way for a leadership challenge against Prime Minister Keir Starmer after months of internal dissent and a catastrophic loss for the party in elections last Thursday. Health Secretary Wes Streeting ended days of speculation by formally resigning from the government in a letter he posted on social media at about 1pm on Thursday in London (about 10pm AEST). Wes Streeting has quit as the UK’s health secretary. Bloomberg But he did not declare his intention to challenge Starmer and focused his statement on his concerns about the government’s direction, leaving doubt around the timing of the next steps to decide who should run the country. Without being specific, he called for a broad contest of candidates to debate the party’s future, in a line that observers regarded as an invitation for other contenders to put their names forward.



A vote by Labour party members could take months to organise, leaving the government divided while ministers argue over the leadership. Another contender for the top post, Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham, is not in the House of Commons, although his supporters claim an MP would give up his or her seat to allow him to run for parliament and enter a leadership contest. Former deputy leader Angela Rayner, who stepped down last year over a tax blunder, told The Guardian she wanted to see change, but she was vague about her intentions. When asked whether Starmer should step aside, she said: “Keir will have to reflect on that.” Streeting made no public comment about his plans in the hour after he released his letter on social media. “Last week’s election results were unprecedented – both in terms of the scale of the defeat and the consequences of that failure,” he wrote in his letter to Starmer.



“You have many great strengths that I admire. You led our party to a victory few thought possible in 2024 and I was proud to fight alongside you in the trenches of that campaign. You have shown courage and statesmanship on the world stage – not least in keeping Britain out of the war in Iran. “But where we need vision, we have a vacuum. Where we need direction, we have drift. This was underscored by your speech on Monday. Leaders take responsibility, but too often that has meant other people falling on their swords. You also need to listen to your colleagues, including backbenchers, and the heavy-handed approach to dissenting voices diminishes our politics.” British Prime Minister Keir Starmer attends the State Opening of Parliament on Wednesday. AP Streeting referred to Starmer’s defence of his record in a major speech on Monday, in the wake of the election results, but he highlighted the challenges facing the country and concluded that Starmer was not up to the task.



“These are big challenges that require a bold vision and bigger solutions than we are offering,” he wrote. “It is now clear that you will not lead the Labour Party into the next general election and that Labour MPs and Labour Unions want the debate about what comes next to be a battle of ideas, not of personalities or petty factionalism. Related Article UK politics King stays calm as Labour lurches into crisis – and challenger emerges “It needs to be broad, and it needs the best possible field of candidates. I support that approach and I hope that you will facilitate this. “Serving as your Secretary of State for Health and Social Care has been the greatest joy of my life and, regardless of our differences this week, I remain truly grateful to you for the opportunity to serve and I am deeply saddened to be leaving government in this way.”



The British press has repeatedly named Streeting as a contender for the prime minister’s job for more than a year, and as recently as May 2 said he had the numbers to launch a challenge. He made no public claim to this, however, and said in his letter that it would have been “dishonourable and unprincipled” to remain in cabinet when he had lost confidence in the prime minister. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Tumult in Westminster reveals an uncomfortable truth for Labour Labour rules state that a challenger must gain support from 20 per cent of the parliamentary party to trigger a challenge. The party has 403 members in the House of Commons, which means Streeting needs 81 to back him in order to trigger a vote by party members to choose the leader. When the party voted on the deputy leadership last year, 87,407 members voted for Lucy Powell – a senior figure on the left – and 73,536 voted for Bridget Phillipson, who was seen as aligned with Starmer.



A poll of Labour members by research firm Survation, and released hours before Streeting’s resignation, found the prime minister would win a vote against the former cabinet minister by 53 per cent to 23 per cent. However, it found that Starmer would lose to Burnham by 28 per cent to 61 per cent. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Taylor goes big in battle to bring Liberal Party back to life
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Taylor goes big in battle to bring Liberal Party back to life Paul Sakkal May 14, 2026 — 9:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

All of a sudden, federal parliament has turned into a big betting parlour. Anthony Albanese’s call to scrap investor tax breaks on Tuesday set off one of the riskiest contests of his prime ministership after years of being labelled timid. All in … Angus Taylor. Alex Ellinghausen Two days on, Angus Taylor has put up big and contentious ideas on tax and migration. Taylor lacks the eye-catching style of colleagues including Andrew Hastie and Matt Canavan, so he had few options but to put a few bold ideas up in lights.



Albanese believes his high-taxing, equality-focused budget will inject new energy into his midterm agenda to avoid drifting as he did in his first term. For Taylor, desperate to get his voice into the public consciousness to counter Pauline Hanson’s headline-grabbing populism, the contest on tax has reminded a confused and downbeat Coalition of its values on lower tax and aspiration. Related Article Federal budget Taylor vows ‘biggest migration cut in Australian history’ and $22.5b worth of tax cuts On tax, Taylor wants to index tax brackets. Peter Dutton shied away from the proposal last term because it was difficult to afford and may not be easily understood by voters. Taylor will use the tax plan to remind One Nation voters of the Coalition’s old strength on economic management. Growth-minded economists, as well as Labor luminary Bill Kelty, support indexation. They argue it would finally take pressure off wage earners after years of flat living standards. Taylor’s decision to repeal Labor’s $100 billion tax hike, should he win the election, exposes him to a fear campaign from Labor on cuts that might be required to plug a budget black hole. Another Coalition policy to lift defence spending will also cost tens of billions, creating questions about how Taylor could possibly make the maths add up.



Taylor said he would cut social security benefits for permanent residents who are not yet citizens. The policy was styled on those of some European nations, some run by left-wing parties, trying to clamp down on migration. Related Article Federal budget Budget fallout: Next tax war will be over rival income tax cuts As a Labor MP pointed out during Taylor’s speech, there are already long wait lists for permanent residents to become citizens. And denying benefits may push people into poverty. Shadow ministers were largely left in the dark about Taylor’s policies, the breadth of which reflects the urgency of his effort to revive a party struggling to retain legitimacy as the chief opposition to Labor. The uncompromising migration plan is driven in significant part by countering One Nation.



Taylor promised substantial migration cuts and claimed he would deport 75,000 people who overstay visas. He did not nominate a migration target, prompting taunts from Labor MPs watching the speech in parliament, and telling the ABC’s 7.30 only that it would be below 200,000. One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce told the program after Taylor’s speech that the opposition leader should “acknowledge One Nation’s policies past, present and emerging”. “It’s game on.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: How Zorko’s absence exposed Lions’ void and announced Cats as a flag favourite
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 How Zorko’s absence exposed Lions’ void and announced Cats as a flag favourite Nick Wright May 15, 2026 — 12:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan has conceded there is a void in his backline in need of filling – one which had a harsh light shone upon it in Dayne Zorko’s absence against Geelong. The veteran was a late scratching from his side’s 17.15 (117) to 11.10 (76) defeat to the Cats on Thursday night, and it appeared to completely shift the way his teammates rallied from the back. Dayne Zorko at a training session in Brisbane on Tuesday. Getty Images Zorko was only two weeks back from a calf concern and withdrawn from the grand final rematch to manage his workload. At 37, he is yet to announce any retirement intentions, and has continued to sign one-year contract extensions since 2022. Fagan hinted managing Zorko’s work would be a regular theme.



“He just pulled up sore from the game last week, and he wasn’t feeling 100 per cent at training on Tuesday, and he wasn’t any better at the captain’s run so we decided not to risk him,” the coach explained. “He’s 37, played 300 games, we’ve [gone] from a Sunday to Saturday to a Friday to a Thursday in the last month, and sometimes that catches up with the older guys, so we just wanted to be careful with him. “You’ve got to be sensible.” Chris Fagan and his Lions have some thinking to do. Getty Images The 311-game star’s career has undergone a renaissance ever since his shift to halfback in 2024. His service – and willingness to attack the corridor – has made the Lions a lethal counter attacking unit.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Privacy and security needs to be lifted’ but McCluggage defends Lions culture Before injury, Zorko had averaged more than 29 touches, four inside 50s and six rebound 50s a game. While Brisbane cruised to wins against Adelaide and Essendon without him, the Cats exposed his void. Aside from a Lions second quarter four-goal blitz – highlighted by two of Charlie Cameron’s three goals for the night, and a brilliant strike from a busy Levi Ashcroft (28 disposals) – Geelong rarely gave up the momentum. In the first quarter alone, they had 23 inside 50s to Brisbane’s eight, with Jeremy Cameron and Bailey Smith in outrageous touch – both kicking freakish snap goals around the body to give their side a 22-point buffer. Coming out of trouble, the Lions targeted the flanks to little avail and such moves were quickly nullified. The Lions’ only two goals both came from the rare occasions they were able to escape their half – 2025 draftee Cody Curtin, fresh off inking a contract extension to the end of 2029, found unmarked by Cam Rayner, before the latter scrambled on a loose ball to strike himself.



Loading Their all-star midfield was kept completely quiet, with Lachie Neale (six first quarter touches) in particular hardly sighted as Geelong rival Oisin Mullin kept him under his watch. Editor's pick Analysis

AFL 2026 The Cats have made a statement. They are the real deal yet again Once Cats forward Shaun Mannagh exploded – kicking five goals along with 30 disposals and three goal assists – there was never a chance of Brisbane mounting a definitive comeback. Four goals in seven minutes early in the third quarter extinguished much of the Lions’ hope. “We lost [Brandon] Starcevich to West Coast and [Noah] Answerth [to concussion] who are good checking defenders. Lincoln McCarthy we tried to develop to that, so the guys who had the job on him [Mannagh] tonight just didn’t get it done,” Fagan said.



“That doesn’t mean to say we can’t make those guys better. We’re asking guys like Jaspa [Fletcher] and Darcy [Wilmot] to play on him, and they’re probably more attacking halfback flankers, so they’ve got to get the balance right in when to attack and when to defend. Related Article NRL 2026 The schools and club talent factories producing the most NRL players “That’s the reality at the moment, we have to develop somebody into that position.” Without Zorko’s influence in generating go-forward, the Lions midfield was deprived of chances to strike, as marquee men Neale, Will Ashcroft (24 disposals) and Hugh McCluggage (16 disposals) were kept contained. In contrast, Mannagh and Smith (two goals, 34 disposals) were at their damaging best, to announce Geelong as serious flag threats and leave the Lions in a period of self-reflection. Not that Fagan is willing to “hit the panic button”, lamenting his side’s 59 per cent kicking efficiency was more a credit to the Cats’ pressure.



“I thought a lot of our really good players didn’t play as well as they normally do. Oisin was tagging Lachie Neale, but I don’t think some of our other mids were getting tagged too closely,” Fagan said. “They just didn’t have good nights. We’ve just won six of our last seven games … we’ve had three or four six-day turnarounds in a row, we just probably need to suck a bit of air in, get a bit of a rest and get ready to go again.” Fagan remained hopeful Zorko, McCarthy and Jarrod Berry could return for next Sunday’s clash with the Giants. World.title: The Cats have made a statement. They are the real deal yet again
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The Cats have made a statement. They are the real deal yet again Peter Ryan May 15, 2026 — 12:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

The Cats will never disappear. All the prayers, predictions and prognostications from opposition supporters have amounted to nothing. Shaun Mannagh celebrates one of his five majors for the night. Getty Images They are still there, nagging away like the lawn you haven’t mowed, the tail-light you haven’t fixed, or the dirty clothes staring back at you from the washing basket. Their demolition of their reigning premiers just five days after smashing Collingwood could be described as a statement, or a brutal reminder, or simply the perfect execution of a well-planned mission.



The club that has played in preliminary finals in eight of the past 10 seasons, and three of the past six grand finals, will be sniffing at the flag again. That’s the only conclusion that can be reached after their Thursday night throttling of the Lions. Bailey Smith and Tanner Bruhn were again influential for Geelong. AFL Photos Cats coach Chris Scott was content with the performance, but knows nothing memorable is won in May. “There is still a lot of footy to be played, but we are confident we will get better,” Scott said.



The Cats’ midfield is supposed to be a weakness but no one worth listening to has got that message through to them yet, except Port Adelaide, anyway. The combination led by young ruckman Mitch Edwards is workmanlike on paper, with rock star Bailey Smith surrounded by bass players in Tom Atkins, Tanner Bruhn, Shaun Mannagh and tagger Oisin Mullin. View post on X Star runner Max Holmes sits in defence to be called upon when needed, while Patrick Dangerfield just marches into the centre if an old and occasionally wise head is needed. Mullin kept dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale quiet, while Hugh McCluggage could not have his normal influence. Will Ashcroft was reasonable, but when Geelong dialled the volume up early in the third quarter none of those stars could be heard over the din as the Cats’ lead stretched to 42 points.



The Cats lost the clearance count but scored 31 more points from clearance than their opposition as they have made that a strength in the past six weeks. Jeremy Cameron kicked three goals for the Cats to take his season tally so far to 27. AFL Photos Mannagh, who was in a rut (a dirty word in some parts) six weeks ago when he described his game against the Hawks on Easter Monday as “a shocker”, has bounced back with vengeance. He was superb in the second half, kicking three goals in a three-minute-and-50-second burst that was perhaps the most exciting sub-four-minute stretch since Roger Bannister ran his famous mile. OK, that might be an exaggeration, but it was a great watch, nonetheless, with two of his goals coming from kicks out of midair. The Lions, with their dwindling supply of small defenders, had no answer. View post on X



One important swing from the grand final was that the Cats had Tom Stewart back in the team, while the Lions were without the injured Dayne Zorko. Stewart, who missed last year’s decider through concussion, intercepted marks and returned anything the Lions could fire inside 50 with interest. He was outstanding. He is commanding a defence that is desperate to keep their foot on their opponents’ throats, while the forward line is predictably unpredictable, with Jeremy Cameron and Shannon Neale the constants inside 50 as the game’s best coach feeds players through the forward half, with Jack Henry making a cameo as he returned from injury. Cameron kicked three to take his season tally to 27, the same number he had after round 10 last year. He finished with 88 goals in 2025. Chris Fagan and his Lions have some thinking to do. Getty Images The Lions will be in contention, too, with their coach Chris Fagan suggesting their hunger for the contest wasn’t as it had been recently with three six-day breaks in a row a potential factor. Justifiably, he said there was no need to “hit the panic button”. Fagan would be well aware the Lions had only lost once to the Cats in their previous five encounters heading into the match. “Well done Geelong. They were great,” he said. The reality is the Cats have been great with monotonous regularity over the past 20 years – their smarts and hard work still the benchmark for most clubs in the competition. They play another team with the same reputation, Sydney, next week at home in a game that will either elevate Geelong’s standing, or confirm the reality they live by, which is that every opponent is tough.



The most ominous comment came from Bailey Smith post-game when he spoke to Channel Seven after another excellent 34-disposal performance. “We don’t want to peak just yet,” Smith said. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.
